articles.text: Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC) hosted its Annual Lunar New Year Celebration at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse this past Friday, February 27, to welcome in the Year of the Horse. Guests enjoyed a bento box dinner with specialty drinks from Tea on Piedmont and artisanal pastries from BakeSum. Piedmont High School’s Troubadours provided a musical performance, and Piedmont Middle School’s karate club showcased their moves on stage. The Lion Dance had drummers providing the musical backdrop as the lions danced across the stage, showcasing their impressive balance. Lunar calendar is based on a combination of lunar and solar movements, with the second new moon after the winter solstice marking the beginning of the new year. The Year of the Horse symbolizes vitality, speed, and perseverance. People born in the Year of the Horse are believed to possess similar traits, such as being hardworking, warm-hearted, and independent. Oppenheimer, a Piedmont resident for nearly 40 years, recently published his 10th book, The Diversity Principle, after 14 years of work and collaboration with more than 100 Berkeley research assistants. Oppenheimer, a clinical professor of law at the University of California, Berkeley School of Law, argues that the modern understanding of diversity began in the late Enlightenment era. Published by Yale University Press, the book reaches beyond law students and legal scholars, the audience for his previous nine publications, to readers interested in the idea, application and history of diversity. “I tell the story through the work and lives of a remarkable group of people who taught us that we make better decisions when we include people with different backgrounds, experiences, and viewpoints,” said Oppenheimer. articles.text: Editor: I was walking my old bones up to the Exedra from Baja Piedmont and sweating like I ate at that one curry restaurant down by the lake on Grand. Since I live at the lowest part of Baja I was quite overheated in the 77 degree weather that is so unseasonal for March let alone February. Who could have imagined that global warming would be so effective? I turned the corner on Magnolia and caught sight of the gleaming new Piedmont Pool, which is going to be ready any month now. I could not stop grinning as I imagined stripping down to the swimsuit I got in southern France back in 1973 and vaulting the fence. Cannonball! Kudos to everyone involved for planning the opening this spring while my health seems to be holding. As I type this with sweaty fingers on my iPhone in Piedmont Park — and recuperate with a $5 sundae as the buzzards look on approvingly from a nearby tree — I am so thankful that I have almost lived to see the new Piedmont Pool open. I can’t wait to dive in! –Ricardo Shibeewah
articles.title: Piedmont’s gleaming new pool

articles.text: Editor: Gray Cathrall’s 90th birthday is more than a personal milestone – it is a civic milestone for everyone who has benefited from his steady, principled presence in our City’s journalism. Plainly said: Piedmont is a better city because of Gray. Not metaphorically better. Concretely better. More honest about itself. More difficult to govern in a good way. More capable of the kind of informed civic argument that healthy communities depend on. These things don’t happen by accident. They happen because someone shows up, year after year, and does the unglamorous work of paying attention on behalf of everyone else. For over two decades, that someone has been Gray. Consider what his presence has meant. When a development project or a budget allocation or a school board policy deserves scrutiny, the Post has provided it. When neighbors needed a common ground — not social media’s battlefield, but a genuine civic commons where ideas meet and facts are checked — the Post has been that place. Without it, Piedmont would be navigating its own affairs with far less transparency and light. Local journalism of this quality is, in much of the country, gone. Piedmont has been spared that. Not because it was lucky, but because Gray chose to build something durable and then protect it. There is also the human dimension of his legacy — the writers he mentored who went on to careers shaped by his example, the readers who came to trust that what they held in their hands was accurate, the sources who learned they could speak to him and be treated fairly. Trust of that kind accumulates slowly. It dissipates quickly. Gray spent 27 years earning it and never a day squandering it. To reach this milestone is remarkable. To reach it having spent a third of it in genuine service to a community — having made that community more transparent, more informed, more capable of self-governance — is something even more rare. Piedmont has been shaped by many people over many decades. Few have shaped it as quietly, as consistently, or as well as Gray Cathrall. Happy 90th birthday, Gray. We are grateful for you every day. (See 90 Things About Gray in the box on page 3.) –Connie & Mark Herrick
articles.title: Celebrating Gray’s 90th

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council formally adopted an updated Local Hazard Mitigation Plan at their meeting on March 2. The plan provides a roadmap showing what Piedmont could do in the coming five years to reduce or avoid potential damages from natural hazards like earthquakes, wildfires, and severe weather. The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) identifies the natural hazards that pose the greatest risk to Piedmont and documents how each hazard would impact Piedmont if it were to occur. The plan identifies and prioritizes actions the City and community could take now that would prevent or reduce those potential impacts. The plan updates Piedmont’s first Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, which was adopted in 2019, to address evolving hazard threats and local conditions. The updated LHMP identifies 30 total actions, 9 that were included in the 2019 LHMP, and 21 new additions that could help reduce risk to Piedmont. The plan’s risk mitigation strategy is to strengthen the resilience of IT infrastructure, retrofit or replace critical facilities to meet modern seismic safety codes, provide annual fire fuel mitigation on city property, and strengthen local building and fire codes to require wildfire-resistant construction. Some of the identified actions, such as strengthening building codes and fire fuel mitigation on City property, have already been completed or are underway. Including an action in the LHMP does not guarantee that it will happen. Rather, it positions the City to apply for state and federal mitigation grants that could support implementing that project. Crafted over a year of research, discussion, and public engagement, the LHMP was submitted to the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services and the Federal Emergency Management Agency for review in fall 2025. The City received notification in January 2026 that the document had passed review and was now eligible for Council adoption. “We are going to take care of problems before the disaster hits, hardening buildings, fixing storm drain infrastructure, working on vegetation management, so we’re all better prepared when a disaster hits, the impact is lower, and we’re able to respond and recover quicker,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. Learn more about the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update process and read the adopted plan at piedmont.ca.gov/LHMP. The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan community workshop that occurred in March 2025. The plan provides a roadmap showing what Piedmont could do in the coming five years to reduce or avoid potential damages from natural hazards like earthquakes, wildfires, and severe weather. The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) identifies the natural hazards that pose the greatest risk to Piedmont and documents how each hazard would impact Piedmont if it were to occur. The plan identifies and prioritizes actions the City and community could take now that would prevent or reduce those potential impacts. The plan updates Piedmont’s first Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, which was adopted in 2019, to address evolving hazard threats and local conditions. The updated LHMP identifies 30 total actions, 9 that were included in the 2019 LHMP, and 21 new additions that could help reduce risk to Piedmont. The plan’s risk mitigation strategy is to strengthen the resilience of IT infrastructure, retrofit or replace critical facilities to meet modern seismic safety codes, provide annual fire fuel mitigation on city property, and strengthen local building and fire codes to require wildfire-resistant construction. Some of the identified actions, such as strengthening building codes and fire fuel mitigation on City property, have already been completed or are underway. Including an action in the LHMP does not guarantee that it will happen. Rather, it positions the City to apply for state and federal mitigation grants that could support implementing that project. Crafted over a year of research, discussion, and public engagement, the LHMP was submitted to the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services and the Federal Emergency Management Agency for review in fall 2025. The City received notification in January 2026 that the document had passed review and was now eligible for Council adoption. “We are going to take care of problems before the disaster hits, hardening buildings, fixing storm drain infrastructure, working on vegetation management, so we’re all better prepared when a disaster hits, the impact is lower, and we’re able to respond and recover quicker,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery will host its 18th Annual Tulip Exhibition at the cemetery’s Tower Chapel, Friday through Sunday, March 20-22, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The free event welcomes in Spring with striking floral arrangements by Bay Area florists, garden clubs, and students from college floral design class. Photographers, florists, flower enthusiasts, and nature and art lovers are welcome. Since its inception in 2006, the cemetery’s annual tulip exhibit has become a cherished community tradition. This year is the exhibit’s third year back after a hiatus due to COVID-19 restrictions. Mountain View Cemetery (5000 Piedmont Avenue) is an historic garden cemetery in the foothills of Oakland and Piedmont. One of the oldest cemeteries in the Western U.S., it has served the community since 1863 and even includes a section for Civil War soldiers. The cemetery was established by a group of East Bay pioneers “Tulips and Dots in Motion” by Agnes Kang from the 2024 Tulip Exhibition under the California Rural Cemetery Act of 1859. Mountain View was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect who also designed New York City’s Central Park, Brooklyn’s Prospect Park, and much of UC Berkeley and Stanford University. For more information on the annual Tulip Exhibition, visit www.mountainviewcemetery. org.
articles.title: 18th Annual Tulip Exhibition returns March 20-22

articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation’s Spring Fling season, themed Palm Royale, is dedicated to the “A” in STEAM, the arts. Enhancements to visual and performing arts programs at Beach, Havens and Wildwood are planned and can be supported at the Palm Royale event on April 25. Piedmont children deserve to learn with musical instruments and art supplies in good repair. As fourth and fifth graders prepare for music theory and string instruction, Spring Fling funds will help ensure there is sufficient sheet music and enough violins. Proceeds also will support arts and crafts classrooms, upgrades to theater productions and instrument repair funds for all grades. The opportunity to fund classroom enhancements, both large and small, outside Piedmont Unified School District’s budget distinguishes Spring Fling from the annual Giving Campaign. Funds raised through the Giving Campaign supplement PUSD’s general budget. “Parent contributions through the annual Giving Campaign help close the gap between what PUSD receives from government funds and what it actually costs to provide each student with an excellent education,” said PEF Executive Director Heather Frank. Funds raised through the Spring Fling season are supplemental to the PUSD budget. Last year, Spring Fling proceeds funded decodable books to support literacy, classroom technology to strengthen computer skills and a contract with Playworks to promote a positive playground experience. This year, elementary parents have the opportunity to expand visual and performing arts programs. “Children love visual and performing arts in our elementary schools, and expanding these programs will provide an amazing opportunity for them to develop creativity and self-expression skills,” said Spring Fling co-chair Monika Riddle. Parents also will have the opportunity to “raise the paddle,” either at the gala or online at PiedmontSpringFling.org, to continue investing in elementary counseling at Beach, Havens and Wildwood. Tickets and sponsorship opportunities are available at PiedmontSpringFling.org.
articles.title: Spring Fling’s Palm Royale raises funds for the arts

Hinkley will present his lecture “Plant Collecting Across the Globe” at UC Berkeley on Saturday, March 28, from 10 to 11 a.m. at the University of California’s Botanical Garden in Julia Morgan Hall. The lecture will highlight plants from Asia, South America, South Africa, New Zealand, and Australia, which are all easily grown in our own local climate. More than 200 of the Botanical Garden’s own accessioned plants are attributed to Dan’s collecting endeavors. This will be an opportunity to hear about Dan’s exploits exploring for plants throughout the world, his gardening life, and his philosophy of gardening and stewardship of legacy gardens. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School (PMS) was named a “2025 California School to Watch” by the California League of Middle Schools (CLMS) with support by the California Department of Education. PMS was one of 90 middle schools selected for the designation, and there are 246 schools of all levels in California with the title. “This program recognizes model middle-grades schools that are academically excellent; developmentally responsive; socially equitable; and led through strong, collaborative leadership,” stated State Superintendent of Public Instruction, Tony Thurmond in a release. The current list includes 46 schools who were added this year and 44 existing Schools to Watch who reapplied. Piedmont Unified School District Superintendent Jennifer Hawn will travel to Long Beach on March 5 for a two-day “Schools to Watch” awards ceremony and district leadership reception. “This prestigious designation reflects the collective efforts of dedicated staff, engaged students, supportive families, and a deeply committed community. At Piedmont Middle School, a shared focus on belonging, high expectations, and student well-being creates an environment where all students are known, supported, and challenged to grow,” said PMS Principal Karyn Shipp. Shipp will make way for current Vice Principal Jamie Van Kleeck to take over the Principal role in July, pending board approval in tonight’s March 4 school board meeting. The statewide 2026 Schools to Watch List will be released later this month.
articles.title: Piedmont Middle School named 2025 California School to Watch

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District will continue to accept nominations for the 2026 Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award until March 13. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. Previous recipients include: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000); Lisa Lomenzo (2001); jointly by Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002); jointly by Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003); Elizabeth (Betsy) Gentry (2004); Cynthia Gorman (2005); Grier Graff (2006); Julia Burke (2007); Maude Pervere (2008); jointly to Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009); Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010); Andrea Swenson (2011), June Monach (2012), Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013), Ray Perman (2014), Jennifer Fox (2015), Katie Korotzer (2016), Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018), Cathy Glazier (2019), Sue Smegal (2020), Ken Li (2021), Eileen Ruby (2022), David Ragones (2023), Sarah Pearson (2024) and most recently, Cory Smegal in 2025. Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982. Art also was very active with the Piedmont Continuation High School (now called Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established in his memory by School Board member Dewey Watson. Nominations for this award are now being sought and will be kept strictly confidential. The deadline for nominations is March 13. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 6, Board of Education meeting, where the honoree’s good works will be acknowledged. articles.text: Piedmont High’s Advanced Acting class will present the acclaimed play Eurydice, by Sarah Ruhl, in the Alan Harvey Theater on Friday, March 6, and Saturday, March 7 at 7:00 p.m. each night. Eurydice is a comedic drama that reimagines the classic myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, focusing on Eurydice’s journey through the Underworld. Reunited with her deceased Grette Willats (left) and Sparrow Lieu prepare for this weekend’s performances of Eurydice during a rehearsal. Mother, Eurydice must grapple with forgotten memories of her past life while facing a life-altering choice. With contemporary characters and plot twists, Eurydice is a fresh look at love and loss. The play is directed by senior Amelia Addington, and the cast includes Yiyou Fang, Kirstin Fedor, Jack Herrlinger, Nico Kaltenecker, Sparrow Lieu, Lila Schwab, and Grette Willats. Addington has been excited to direct the show because of its creative and poetic natures. “Its abstract storytelling and emotional depth allow both the cast and the audience to interpret the story in different and personal ways,” she said. With nearly 20 plays and a MacArthur Genius Grant to her name, author Sarah Ruhl is one of the most important American playwrights of our time. The Advanced Acting Class has previously produced her shows, Dead Man’s Cell Phone and The Clean House. Eurydice has been produced from high schools to Broadway, and it has been translated into 14 languages. In 2021, Ruhl adapted Eurydice into an Opera that ran during the New York Metropolitan Opera Season. Eurydice is recommended for most audiences, though some material may not be suitable for younger audience members. This production explores themes of love, loss, memory, and the afterlife. It is always encouraged that audiences use their best judgment based on the show’s themes and the child’s age and maturity level. Contact producer Kimberly Taylor, at ktaylor@ piedmont.k12.ca.us, with any questions. Tickets are $5 for students and $10 for general admission. Tickets can be purchased at phsacting. ludus.com.

articles.text: & Kaito Ciammaichella Piedmont’s Troop 1 Scouts received a behind the scenes look at how local news is made - from the use of robotic cameras to the teamwork involved in getting video and news on the air. On February 14, fifteen Scouts took a tour of the KTVU studios in Oakland’s Jack London Square. At the start of the tour, the Scouts were invited onto the set of KTVU’s “Take 2 This Morning” streaming show. The Scouts were interviewed by anchors Allie Rasmus and Frank Mallicoat. Mallicoat told the troop members he is an Eagle Scout—the highest ranking one can earn in scouting. He talked to the troop about all the beneficial skills he gained from his scouting experience. “I learned so much, like leadership, working as a team, cooking, camping, taking care of myself and others, reaching goals, and being responsible,” said Mallicoat. “I’m still friends with a number of my fellow Scouts even 50 years later.” Members of the troop also toured the KTVU control room. They learned how the audio, video, and other equipment operate and spoke with news producers and directors about their roles. “The most surprising thing I learned is that the cameras in the studio were unmanned and moved by themselves,” said Scout, Kian Spina. “The studio was like a finetuned machine, with everyone depending on everyone,” added Scout Ozzie Edelson-Evans. Some Scouts had the opportunity to sit in the director’s chair and change all the different camera angles, backgrounds, and screen editing. Afterwards, some Scouts read from the teleprompter to experience part of the job of a news anchor. “We learned about the role of the producer and how they must crunch all the different interviews and squeeze all the times together, so it all fits into the one news report,” said Scout Adrien Messina. The Scouts learned had the chance to observe how the green screen works. The screen is a chromakey software program used by meteorologists to display weather satellite maps and 5-day forecasts. If someone wears the color green in front of the screen, the satellite image will appear on their clothing. Scouts used a green tablecloth to see what it was like to “disappear” into the green screen. “Everything green showed weather on it, so Allie gave us a green piece of fabric and everything under it disappeared!” said Troop 1 Scout Kaito Ciammaichella. “It showed me it takes a lot of work to put on the news.” The Scouts had a revelatory experience into the innerworkings of television. “It really opened my eyes, and it’s something I would have never seen without Scouts,” said Troop member Cormac Hoffmam. articles.text: Assistant Scoutmaster Troop 1 Piedmont Scouts in Troop 1 set out on their Urban Backpacking/ Kirby Cove Service Project outing on February 27. The annual trip takes place one week before Kirby Cove Campground opens for the 2026 season. Given the mid-winter timing, this adventure often unfolds under gray skies, gusty winds, and occasional rain. Not this year. The skies were blue, the sun was out, and barely a breeze, making for a perfect day for a hike. Getting to Kirby Cove Recreation Area, one of the crown jewels of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, makes up most of the adventure. Starting in Piedmont, the troop rode AC Transit’s Route 88 bus to downtown Oakland, then walked a mile to Jack London Square to board the ferry to the San Francisco Ferry Building. This year, with the Pier 41 Short Hop Ferry no longer in service, Scouts added an extra mile to their route, hiking from the Ferry Building to Pier 39. A favorite tradition soon followed: a stop at Boudin Bakery at Fisherman’s Wharf, where Scouts refueled with sourdough bread, cheese bread, and other well-earned treats. From there, the group continued on foot through Fort Mason and Crissy Field, pausing at the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy’s Warming Hut before making the climb to the Golden Gate Bridge. For several Scouts and adult leaders, it was their first time crossing the bridge on foot, accompanied by sweeping views of the bay. After taking in the scenery at Vista Point in Marin County, the troop began the final descent down the trail to Kirby Cove near the base of the Golden Gate Bridge. In total, the Scouts covered eight miles of stunning vistas, varied terrain, and the kind of camaraderie that turns shared miles into shared memories. articles.text: Here’s a question worth asking at your next family dinner: What do a bike wheel, a clock, and a pizza have in common? The answer is a number your older kids have probably met in math class—one that’s been quietly running the show all around them since before they could count. That number is Pi. Pi (written as the Greek letter π) is the ratio of any circle’s circumference (the distance around it) to its diameter (the distance across). This means if you divide the distance all the way around a circle by the distance across it through the center, you’ll always get a number around 3.14 (or Pi). It works for every circle, everywhere, without exception, whether pizza, plate, or planet. That consistency is what makes Pi remarkable. It’s one of the most important numbers in mathematics, art, nature, technology, and so many other industries. articles.text: Piedmont High’s No. 3 seeded girls’ basketball team took home third-place in the North Coast Section Open Division, beating No. 4 Clayton Valley Charter 58-53 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, February 27. Two days earlier, the Highlanders lost 52-39 to No. 2 Carondelet, which went on to beat No. 1 San Ramon Valley for the title. On Tuesday, March 3, PHS received the No. 3 seed in the CIF State Division 1 bracket and faced No. 14 Antelope for the third time this season Results were not complete by Post time. “We’re working hard right now and the girls are doing what we ask. The bigger games we’re in, the higher the stakes; you realize every possession is important. We need every point and rebound we get,” coach Bryan Gardere said. There were 16 total lead changes in the game with Clayton Valley. Piedmont trailed 53-49 lead with 2:45 left in the game. But from that point on, the Highlanders didn’t allow another basket. “The energy in the room changed, My teammates and I knew what we had to do to get the win. Our competitiveness changed, we just wanted it more,” junior Taylor White said. Converting shots at the free throw line proved to be a critical piece of the win. The Highlanders converted 21 of 26 free throws, including 11 of 12 in the fourth quarter. “Free throws are something we’ve been crying about as coaches. We had them try to Staff Photos Jenelle Solis celebrates with coach Bryan Gardere after Piedmont’s win over Clayton Valley Charter. shoot at lunch time, after practice, and we shot a lot in yesterday’s practice. The more reps, the better,” Gardere said. “We have set goals and we always try to get above 70 percent. That’s something we’ve been working toward all year,” sophomore guard Jenelle Solis said. 58-52 victory over Clayton Valley Charter Piedmont led 17-16 through the first quarter, including five lead changes when Solis landed a shot with five seconds left. The back-and-forth scoring continued in the second quarter with five lead changes through the opening three minutes. CVC pushed its lead to 30-24, but PHS closed with baskets by Andrea Martin and White to cut the deficit to 30-28 at halftime. In the third quarter, Piedmont went up 36-35 at the 3:52 mark. Taylor White logged 21 rebounds in Piedmont’s win over Clayton Valley Charter. Andrea Martin led with 25 points on Clayton Valley. CVC went up 50-45 midway through the quarter, but PHS chipped away to 50-49. Clayton Valley hit a 3-pointer with 2:45 left, 53-49, but the Highlanders followed with a 9-0 scoring run to end the game. It started with White grabbing an offensive rebound and assisting Martin, a free throw by Martin, and a bucket by Solis to take the lead 54-53 with 1:15 left. Final stats: Martin had 13 points, seven rebounds, one assist. Be had 11 points, four rebounds, one assist, and one steal. Johnson had six points, three rebounds, and two steals. Piedmont High’s baseball team got its season underway in big fashion with a dominant 10-1 win over Skyline on the Titans’ home field in the Oakland Hills on Friday, February 27. Piedmont undergoes big changes from last year’s team that reached the North Coast Section quarterfinals as the No. 2 seed. Still, coach Eric Olson is excited about the returning team. “I looked around and we have some new guys in starting roles, but we also have guys who are back and guys who have bigger roles than last year,” Olson said. Piedmont’s infield is among the reasons for Olson’s optimism. To get out there and train with him every day is a dream come true. He deserves the opportunity and works just as hard as I do,” Diego said. “Since I was in middle school, I’ve been dreaming about teaming up with my brother. It’s really cool. articles.text: As things go in youth sports in Piedmont, kids build friendships and connections on the fields and in gyms that they may take with them for the first of their lives. With this year’s Piedmont High baseball team, seniors Diego Delventhal and Jack Meyjes embark on their final season playing together before graduating with the Class of 2026, ending a tradition they’ve largely continued since their tee-ball days when they were five-years-old. Delventhal and Meyjes have been teammates on Piedmont High’s varsity baseball team for four years. Delventhal has been a second baseman and shortstop, while Meyjes has been an infielder and pitcher. Following graduation this spring, Meyjes will be off to continue his baseball career at Bates College while Delventhal will head to Pitzer College. “It started back in tee-ball; he was the first person I made friends with,” said Meyjes. “Throughout our elementary school years, we were always on the same team. We always stuck together.” They’ve seen success both on the school’s team and during their little league days. Playing on the Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation’s Pinto league for ages 7-8, the two won a championship game where Meyjes hit the walk-off winner to lift the trophy. “We were in Pinto and he came up with the bases loaded in a tie game. He hit a walk-off to win the championship down the right field line,” Delventhal recalled. “We won a couple of Piedmont championships. It was our second year in Pinto That was probably in the second grade, I just remember celebrating with him, his dad, and my dad,” Meyjes said On the high school team, the pair has been a key part of recent success. The Highlanders reached the 2023 North Coast Section semifinals as the No. 8 seed as freshmen. As sophomores, they were runners up in the 2024 NCS championship and CIF State D4 championship after winning the WACC Foothill regular season title, They were last year’s No. 2 seed in the NCS Div. 3 postseason and reached the quarterfinals. In 2024 as sophomores, Meyjes was the winning pitcher when Piedmont wpm the league championship (WACC Foothill), clinching a 7-5 win over Berkeley. “I remember when he closed it out to win league and we all congregated at the mound to celebrate. That was dope,” Delventhal said of his favorite high school memory of Jack. Piedmont undergoes big changes from last year’s team that reached the North Coast Section quarterfinals as the No. 2 seed. Still, coach Eric Olson is excited about the returning team. “I looked around and we have some new guys in starting roles, but we also have guys who are back and guys who have bigger roles than last year,” Olson said. Piedmont’s infield is among the reasons for Olson’s optimism. The middle of the infield will have senior Diego Delventhal at shortstop having the rare opportunity to play alongside his younger brother, Lucas Delventhal, at second base. “It’s always been a dream of mine. To get out there and train with him every day is a dream come true. He deserves the opportunity and works just as hard as I do,” Diego said. “Since I was in middle school, I’ve been dreaming about teaming up with my brother. It’s really cool. I’ve been prepared to play and I let my play do the talking today. Hopefully I can stay hot,” mentioned Lucas. Diego Delventhal, Jack Meyjes embark on final baseball season together By Jonathan Comeaux As things go in youth sports in Piedmont, kids build friendships and connections on the fields and in gyms that they may take with them for the first of their lives. With this year’s Piedmont High baseball team, seniors Diego Delventhal and Jack Meyjes embark on their final season playing together before graduating with the Class of 2026, ending a tradition they’ve largely continued since their tee-ball days when they were five-years-old. Delventhal and Meyjes have been teammates on Piedmont High’s varsity baseball team for four years. Delventhal has been a second baseman and shortstop, while Meyjes has been an infielder and pitcher. Following graduation this spring, Meyjes will be off to continue his baseball career at Bates College while Delventhal will head to Pitzer College. “It started back in tee-ball; he was the first person I made friends with,” said Meyjes. “Throughout our elementary school years, we were always on the same team. We always stuck together.” They’ve seen success both on the school’s team and during their little league days. Playing on the Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation’s Pinto league for ages 7-8, the two won a championship game where Meyjes hit the walk-off winner to lift the trophy. “We were in Pinto and he came up with the bases loaded in a tie game. He hit a walk-off to win the championship down the right field line,” Delventhal recalled. “We won a couple of Piedmont championships. It was our second year in Pinto That was probably in the second grade, I just remember celebrating with him, his dad, and my dad,” Meyjes said On the high school team, the pair has been a key part of recent success. The Highlanders reached the 2023 North Coast Section semifinals as the No. 8 seed as freshmen. As sophomores, they were runners up in the 2024 NCS championship and CIF State D4 championship after winning the WACC Foothill regular season title, They were last year’s No. 2 seed in the NCS Div. 3 postseason and reached the quarterfinals. In 2024 as sophomores, Meyjes was the winning pitcher when Piedmont wpm the league championship (WACC Foothill), clinching a 7-5 win over Berkeley. “I remember when he closed it out to win league and we all congregated at the mound to celebrate. That was dope,” Delventhal said of his favorite high school memory of Jack. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team has returned for its 2026 season, having already played its first two matches of the season. The Highlanders lost 15-8 at Foothill on Tuesday, February 24 and fell 10-7 to Campolindo at Witter Field two days later. PHS is back after reaching last year’s Division 2 North Coast Section championship game, finishing as runners up to College Park in an 8-7 overtime loss. That team featured 14 seniors from the Class of 2025, meaning this year’s squad inherently has some huge changes. “We’ve barely had a week of practice and played a decent Foothill team. From that game to Campolindo, these girls really figured it out,” coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont has to replace Friedie Schickedanz, whose role was to hold up the ball near the net as a playmaking scorer and assister. Still, PHS brings back the Post’s honorable mention for Athlete of the Year, Peyton Watson. Hallie Burden is another returning player poised for a big role after missing the entire 2025 season due to an injury. “It’s a whole new roster. Hallie didn’t play all last year and is now taking the draw. We have Peyton, and most of our girls were on JV last year. We basically have a few seasoned varsity girls who are pulling along their younger teammates,” Chan said. Last season, Piedmont faced struggles during the early portion of the schedule in moving the ball up field as they transitioned defense into attack. There was a similar tone in 2026’s opening two games, but PHS found its groove in the second quarter against Campolindo. “We told them that the Campolindo game was going to be a lot faster. What we did was go back to fundamentals, spread out, make the back pass, and trust each other,” Chan said. 10-7 loss to Campolindo Campolindo led 5-1 through the first quarter and Piedmont trailed 8-4 by halftime. Campo extended its lead to 9-4 through the third quarter, while the Highlanders scored three in the fourth and only conceded one. Piedmont scored the game’s opening goal after a minute and a half, but the Cougars went on to score five straight goals. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont Unified School District hosted a meeting to examine fan conduct at games following a brawl after a basketball game on January 30. On January 30, a shocking altercation between Piedmont High’s students and the visiting San Leandro boys’ basketball team players and coaches made the KTVU News. It was a moment that preceded two other incidents from high school athletics to make larger headlines; a racial slur being hurled at an Arizona high school basketball game on February 20, and De La Salle in Concord announcing on February 25 that they are suspending their baseball team for the first five games of its season based on conduct violations. To call attention to appalling behavior at sports events throughout the country, Piedmont Unified School District hosted a fan conduct meeting on Thursday, February 26 to talk with Piedmont parents about concerns regarding the January 30 brawl. “This is a topic that is certainly in the news.; we know school districts run into problems, whether it be the athletes themselves or spectator conduct. We’ve had some bumps in the road as well, so we want to get out in front of this issue,” Superintendent Jennifer Hawn said. Piedmont High athletic director Tyler Small and principal David Yoshihara discussed certain models and protocols they would like to use going forward, noting that accountability for adults in attendance is also important. “A lot about this is us as a district and high school holding a high standard. Tyler and I are at a lot of events and see student interactions, as well as adult interactions. It’s one thing to work with students, but it’s also difficult to see how some adults behave, because I do know the students are watching,” Yoshihara said. Yoshihara made sure to mention that their goal is to have great play appreciated, regardless if the team is the home or away side. “We want to acknowledge great play regardless of what team. We want it to be exciting, we want it to be loud. Loudness is okay, it’s what we choose to say. “Go Highlanders” is okay, but if we’re antagonizing the other team, we have to figure out where we draw those lines,” Yoshihara said. Yoshihara listed things that will no longer be acceptable. include students or fans calling out opposing players by name, number, hair styles, attire, or anything identifying a specific player. Tyler later mentioned that there could be some collaboration with Western Alameda County Conference schools to streamline new rules to help prevent students from rushing the fields or courts after wins. Hawn acknowledged that the conduct of Piedmont’s players has been stellar, evident by the boys’ basketball team completely avoiding the fracas on January 30. The issue, as evident on that January night, was with spectators and coaches of the opposing team. “The conduct of our athletes are typically excellent. I think it’s the fan conduct, both the adults and sometimes students, where we have some work to do. But we can do it, we can absolutely do it. That’s why we’re here, to reset expectations and bring in the community to help us with this,” Hawn said. One topic of debate has been whether the school will bring in additional security for night games. When asked if it’s important to have more security at big events, knowing kids storming onto fields of play to celebrate is a typical tradition in sports, Hawn responded: “I don’t think it is a dramatic safety issue. I think it’s probably a communication of expectations and maybe some amount of an accountability issue.” PUSD is examining preventing fans from rushing fields of play following a notice from the State.

articles.text: The Piedmont High School Mountain Bike Team opened the 2026 NorCal League season at Fort Ord with two podium finishes and a 4th-place overall team standing in a field of 435 high school racers. On a fast, sandy 4-mile course that grew looser throughout the day, riders had to balance power with patience. Senior Jasper Schuetz finished 2nd in Varsity Boys in 1:09:31, delivering five steady laps and averaging over 300 watts in a powerful early-season performance. Sophomore Josephine Schuetz won the JV2 Girls race in 59:14, breaking the one-hour mark and claiming the leader’s jersey with a margin of more than two minutes. Piedmont also saw strong finishes from Zachary Carter (6th, JV1 Boys D2), Rose Reining (6th, JV2 Girls), and Caleb Canada (10th, JV2 Boys D2), contributing to a deep and balanced team result. The team’s strength ran deep, with Mina Herrgott, Olivia Bailey, Kai Hsu, Gabriel Barbosa, Asher Villarreal, Henry Call, Emilio Roberts, and Chase Mellers all delivering determined efforts in highly competitive divisions. The strength of Piedmont MTB extends beyond the high school team. articles.text: Treasure Island Museum is adding a second public art gallery including works by artists featured at the 1939 and 1940 Golden Gate International Exposition. The new gallery opens this Saturday, March 7, in the museum’s historic Building One and includes paintings, drawings, sculptures, lithographs and more by California artists, displayed publicly for the first time in decades since the groundbreaking exposition. The gallery will feature rotating exhibitions showcasing artwork preserved by the Spencer Jon Helfen Collection, offering visitors a glimpse into the island’s unique past and significance in the San Francisco Bay Area’s history and future. The museum was established in 1975 and opened to the public in 1976. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and has served as a Pan American Airways terminal and naval headquarters in addition to an exposition hub. Treasure Island Museum’s mission is to preserve and interpret the island’s Pacific-themed heritage, educate residents and visitors on its historical relevance to contemporary issues, support community partnerships and inspire future generations through programs, exhibitions and events. The gallery opening is held on March 7, 12 p.m. to 3 p.m. at 39 Treasure Island Rd #111 in San Francisco. The event is free but registration is required. Visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/gallery-opening to learn more and to register online. articles.text: J.Miller Flowers and Gifts arrangement at Legion of Honor For 26 years, sisters Valerie and Robin Lee have marked the arrival of spring not just with blossoms in their shop windows, but with an installation at one of the Bay Area’s most anticipated museum traditions. The co-owners of J.Miller Flowers and Gifts are once again among more than 120 floral designers participating in the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s annual Bouquets to Art exhibition, which runs through Sunday, March 8. The weeklong event pairs arrangements with works from the permanent collections and architecture of the de Young Museum and the Legion of Honor. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse presents the Tony Award-winning musical Once opening February 21 and running through March 8. Featuring a book by Enda Walsh and music and lyrics by Glen Hansard and Markéta Irglová, Once is based on the 2007 film that earned the Academy Award for Best Original Song for “Falling Slowly.” Set in Dublin, the story follows an Irish busker and a Czech immigrant who form a deep connection through music during a life-changing week of songwriting and collaboration. The production is directed by Josh Marx, with music direction by Michael Patrick Wiles and choreography by Erin Rose Solorio. Actors perform their own instruments onstage, creating a pub-style atmosphere that underscores the show’s themes of community and artistic partnership. “I’ve always loved Once because it digs into something I think about a lot: what music really is and how it connects us Photo by Ben Krantz Jake Gale and Gillian Eichenberger perform in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Once. as human beings,” Marx said. “I loved the movie Once when I first saw it— and then the Broadway production pulled me in even deeper, especially the way it evoked a sense of community; similar to drinking a pint of Guinness in an Irish pub while patrons play music together. For Berkeley Playhouse’s production, we’re looking to put something truly special together; each actor plays their own instrument (sometimes more than one!), and we want to create an unforgettable experience that capitalizes on the amazing talent that we’re bringing into the room.” Jake Gale and Gillian Eichenberger lead the cast as Guy and Girl. For tickets or more information, call (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Cal Performances The opera merges Jean Cocteau’s 1946 romantic fantasy with Philip Glass’ 1994 score. Opera Parallèle will present two major productions this Spring, with a revival of its critically-acclaimed production of La Belle et la Bête showing Friday, March 13, and Saturday, March 14, both at 8 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. Based on Jean Cocteau’s 1946 film and set to Philip Glass’s 1994 score, the production fuses live performance with film imagery in a surrealist retelling of the classic fairy tale. Nicole Paiement conducts, with direction and production concept by Brian Staufenbiel. The creative team also includes projection designer and director of photography David Murakami, lighting designer Jessica Ann Drayton, costume designer Natalie Barshow, hair and makeup designer Y. Sharon Peng, and sound designer Jay Cruz. Sung in French with projected English supertitles, the approximately 90-minute opera runs without intermission. The cast features Hadleigh Adams as La Bête, Le Prince, Avenant and l’Officier; Chea Kang as La Belle; Aurélien Mangwa as Le Père, Ludovic and L’Usurier; and Sophie Delphis as Félicie and Adélaïde. Tickets start at $55. Later in the season, Opera Parallèle presents the West Coast opera debut of Doubt, with music by Douglas Cuomo and a libretto by John Patrick Shanley. The opera will be staged in partnership with Presidio Theatre, with performances Friday, May 29, and Saturday, May 30, at 7:30 p.m., and Sunday, May 31, at 3 p.m., at Presidio Theatre in San Francisco. Based on Shanley’s Pulitzer Prize- and Tony Award-winning play, Doubt is sung in English with projected English supertitles and runs approximately 100 minutes without intermission. These performances introduce a new chamber orchestra version created by the composer and an abridged libretto by Kevin Newbury. Paiement conducts with Staufenbiel directing. The cast includes Matthew Worth as Father Flynn, Rhoslyn Jones as Sister Aloysius, Naomi Steele as Sister James, and Deborah Nansteel as Mrs. Miller. Tickets start at $66.

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet School will celebrate decades of artistic leadership this spring with a galastyle festival at the War Memorial Opera House, marking the first time the school’s Spring Festival will be staged in the historic venue with live orchestral accompaniment. The 2025 Spring Festival, set for May 9 and 10, features works by past and present artistic directors of San Francisco Ballet, including Helgi Tomasson, Michael Smuin, Lew Christensen and current San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo. Students will perform to live music by the Grammy Award-winning San Francisco Ballet Orchestra under Music Director and Principal Conductor Martin West. The program, curated by School Director Grace Holmes, includes excerpts from Rojo’s “Raymonda,” Tomasson’s “Handel – A Celebration,” Smuin’s “Quattro a Verdi,” Christensen’s “Vivaldi Concerto Grosso” and August Bournonville’s “La Sylphide.” “This program is a testament to the legacy, evolution, and enduring artistry that defines San Photo by Lindsay Thomas San Francisco Ballet School Students in 2024 Spring Festival Francisco Ballet and San Francisco Ballet School,” Holmes said in a press release. “It is an honor to celebrate the innovation and creativity that continue to inspire generations of dancers and audiences on a global scale. We are proud to be able to give these students the opportunity to perform in a venue with such a rich legacy alongside the unparalleled SF Ballet Orchestra as our students continue to develop artistically and strive toward professional careers in ballet.” Additional works include a world premiere by company member Davide Occhipinti and the West Coast debut of Esteban Hernández’s “1941,” both commissioned through the organization’s Creation House initiative supporting emerging choreographers. Performances are scheduled for 7 p.m. May 9 and 4 p.m. May 10. Tickets start at $29, with discounted children’s tickets available. Proceeds will support scholarships and education programs serving more than 40,000 community members annually. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ support-engage/special-events/ to purchase tickets online. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony will open its 2026 Chamber Series with four curated programs highlighting contemporary voices and classical masterworks, all held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The series begins with “Roots and Resonances” on February 22 at 4 p.m., curated by composer Samuel Adams. The program features percussionist Haruka Fujii and a string quartet from the symphony in works exploring texture and timbre, including music by Salina Fisher and Osvaldo Golijov, as well as Adams’ “Sundial” and Fujii’s “Divisions.” On March 22, “French Connections,” curated by Dianne Nicolini of Classical California KDFC, will feature works by Francis Poulenc, Lili Boulanger and Gabriel Fauré. Composer Juan Pablo Contreras curates “The Music of Muses” on April 12, with music by Reena Esmail, Jennifer Higdon and Bedřich Smetana, alongside his “Musas Mexicanas.” The series concludes May 31 with “I, Too, Sing America,” curated by James Parrish Smith, featuring works by Brian Raphael Nabors, Anna Clyne and Antonín Dvořák. The symphony closes its 2025/26 season following the conclusion of Music Director Joseph Young’s successful sixyear tenure. “This season represents an exciting new chapter for Berkeley Symphony,” said Berkeley Symphony Executive Director Marion Atherton in a press release. “We’re thrilled to welcome some of today’s most compelling conductors, each bringing their unique artistic vision to our stage.” This season “shines a light on stirring masterpieces from the classical canon alongside groundbreaking contemporary works,” Atherton added. “From Dvorák’s lyrical Eighth Symphony to Shostakovich’sspirited Ninth and Haydn’s vivid ‘Military’ Symphony, we’re exploring rich musical territory beyond the standard repertoire while showcasing the versatility and excellence of our orchestra.” Chamber Series subscriptions are $120 and available through the symphony’s box office and website. Subscriptions can be purchased by calling the box office at (510) 841-2800 or visiting berkeleysymphony.org. The symphony returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Spring. articles.text: Mason Thames in How to Train Your Dragon There are stories that endure because they tap something we recognize before we can name it — the outcast, the misunderstood creature, the friendship that costs something. How to Train Your Dragon, now reimagined in live action, knows exactly what kind Adapted from the animated franchise, itself drawn from Cressida Cowell’s books, the film returns us to the Viking village of Berk, where dragons are feared, hunted and poorly understood. At the center is Hiccup, a slight, thoughtful boy born into a culture that prizes brute strength. He is the chief’s son who cannot become his father. Into this comes Toothless — a Night Fury, the most feared dragon in the skies — injured, grounded, and just as stranded from the world as the boy who finds him. What begins as secrecy becomes friendship. What begins as fear becomes trust. When Hiccup looks into a dragon’s eyes and sees something like himself, he cannot go through with the kill. That moment of recognition — quiet, almost accidental — is where the film lives. The dragon who has every reason to destroy humans learns, slowly, to depend on one. What DeBlois has always understood — as the writer-director of the original trilogy, now returned to remake his own work — is that Hiccup is not learning to tame a dragon. He is learning to see one. His village’s hatred is not mere superstition; it is inherited identity, passed down so long it feels like instinct. To question it is to become a stranger in your own home. DeBlois never lets Hiccup off easily, and never lets the audience mistake recognition for resolution. The live-action finds textures the animation could only suggest. The flying sequences are exhilarating, but it is the stillness that lingers — a wordless early encounter where Hiccup and Toothless circle each other, neither willing to look away, each unsure whether to run. Wind moves through Viking fur cloaks. Scales catch real light. Berk feels inhabited rather than constructed. The outsider, this film keeps insisting, sees what the tribe has trained itself not to. It is an old idea. DeBlois makes you feel it anyway. How to Train Your Dragon. Directed by Dean DeBlois. Starring Mason Thames, Nico Parker, Gerard Butler. Released in 2025. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG. articles.text: Flow is one of those films I genuinely regret not seeing sooner. It won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature in 2025, and once I finally sat down with it, I understood why. The film is built on a technology called Blender, a free, open-source 3D creation suite that gives animators a painterly, almost impressionistic visual style. I’ll be honest: when people start explaining “core animation technology,” my eyes glaze over. But none of that matters once the film begins. What unfolds on screen is lush, detailed, and immediately absorbing. The story follows a black cat living alone in an abandoned house deep in the forest. There’s no dialogue, no narration, just sound. Animal noises. Barking. The cat’s soft mewing. The filmmakers have to make you care about this creature without a single spoken word, and somehow, they pull it off. Things get moving when a massive flood tears through the forest, almost Biblical in scale. The cat, who we come to know as Flow, is swept up along with everything else. The hope, such as it is, becomes finding dry land. What Flow finds instead is a small sailboat carrying an odd collection of survivors: lemurs, a dog, a large white stork-like bird, a capybara. None of them especially want to share the space. All of them have to do it. There’s an environmental undercurrent running through the whole film, though it never turns preachy. More striking is what the filmmakers chose not to do. The animals aren’t anthropomorphized. They don’t speak or reason like humans. articles.text: The Oakland Zoo has welcomed a new red-tailed monkey baby boy! The Zoo’s resident red-tailed guenons, Nonami the mother and Marley the father, welcomed a male offspring in February. The milestone marks the first birth of a guenon monkey at Oakland Zoo. Nonami and her baby boy, named Tumbili, are thriving. He is nursing and bonding normally with Nonami, and she is ensuring the baby stays close. As a veteran mom, Nonami has successfully given birth at her previous Zoo to two other females who also live at Oakland Zoo: Ikea and Skittles. Nonami and her baby have joined the rest of the troop in their habitat, and the baby’s sister, Ikea, has shown strong interest in her brother and wants to help Mom with grooming while Nonami supervises. Mom and baby frequently spend time in the habitat, where visitors can see them every day, but sometimes Mom may prefer to retreat to a cozy, warm bedroom space with her baby. Nonami and Marley were recommended for breeding by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) within the Guenon Red-tailed Monkey Species Survival Plan (SSP). The SSP was created by the AZA (which accredits Oakland Zoo) to promote the sustainability of a healthy, genetically diverse, and demographically varied AZA population. Keepers are thrilled about the Nonami, one of Oakland Zoo’s resident red-tailed guenons, and her new baby boy, Tumbili.

articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and a lively discussion afterward. The Flix Fest’s March selection is 400 Blows, directed by Francois Truffaut. This film was his first New Wave film as a director and is considered an autobiographical portrayal of his own adolescent years. The film takes place in 1959 in the urban cityscape of Paris. Using a hand-held camera, Truffaut follows the adventures of 12-year-old Antoine Doinel, with a mixture of outdoor and static scenes of his apartment and classroom. Antoine’s artistic interests are curtailed by a rigid French curriculum focused on the written word, and his emotional development is stunted at home by unloving parents, who treat him as a nuisance in their adult lives. These restrictions lead Antoine to rebel against his teacher in class and his parents at home with acts of mischief and truancy, as he searches for freedom of expression with his best friend from school. The theft of a typewriter from his father’s office results in a night in jail and a 2-month stay at a juvenile detention center for boys, requested by his parents, who no longer know how to control his behavior. articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest is back for a fifth year! articles.text: It all started with a simple idea: what if busy families could have a dedicated handyman they could count on — no flaking, no chasing, no stress? For Avantika Prabhakara and her husband Vishwas, Lafayette parents of three, that idea wasn’t on the radar… until their neighbors gave them a chance. “Building a home maintenance company with my wife, Avantika, was never the plan,” Vishwas says. “But after an irrigation specialist took a hefty deposit and completely ghosted us, we realized how common and frustrating that experience was. With a small group of neighbors willing to take a chance on something new, that’s how Honey Homes got started.” Back in 2022, 15 Beta members in Lafayette said yes to a brand-new concept: a dedicated handyman for your home. Not a one-off contractor, but someone reliable, consistent, and invested in your house year-round. Those early families helped shape everything — from dependable scheduling to thoughtful, family-friendly service designed specifically for busy households. Four years later, Honey Homes now supports over 400 families in Piedmont and over 3,000 families across the Bay Area, Los Angeles, Dallas, Austin, and Chicago. For Piedmont homeowners, that means help with everything from mounting garage racks, hanging blackout shades in sunny rooms, tightening loose fixtures, or pressure-washing front walkways along Highland Avenue. Honey Homes is all about helping families reclaim time, energy, and peace of mind. In a community known for beautiful historic homes and full family calendars, Honey Homes is designed to help families protect their homes — and reclaim their time. “What started as a neighborhood experiment has become a community of families counting on us for more comfort, more joy, and a lot less stress at home,” Avantika says. Thank you to Piedmont To celebrate the community that has embraced Honey Homes, the team is giving back. Ten Piedmont neighbors will receive a complimentary Honey Homes trial — including a personalized planning walk-thru and 1.5 hours of dedicated handyman help to tackle those lingering to-dos. articles.text: Earlier this year on January 31, wine lovers gathered in downtown San Jose for the Festival of Undiscovered Grapes, an immersive wine-tasting celebration highlighting the world’s rare and lesser-known grape varieties. The event drew local residents and visitors eager to explore beyond familiar varietals like Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, and Pinot Noir. Instead, guests sipped wines made from “underdog” grapes — including Semillon, Teroldego, Tannant, Bourbolenc, Cinsault, and Trousseau — representing more than 110 unique winegrape varieties grown in California. With dozens of wineries pouring their distinctive selections, attendees wandered the room sampling bold reds, aromatic whites, and intriguing blends that many had never encountered before. Wine producers from across the state were on hand to share stories of their vineyards and the heritage of these lesser-known grapes, offering insight into the diversity of California’s wine landscape. Participants could choose between general admission and VIP tickets. VIP guests enjoyed early access, a pre-tasting discussion focused on Lodi wine varietals with experts, a commemorative wine glass, and complimentary delivery of bottles ordered at the event. General admission ticket holders joined the tasting after the VIP session and had the option to have their wine purchases delivered for a flat fee. A food vendor on site offered small bites and snacks to pair with the wines, creating a festive atmosphere throughout the afternoon. Conversations flowed as easily as the pours, with many oenophiles excited to discover new favorites and broaden their palates. Organizers said the festival aimed not just to entertain but to educate, spotlighting vinicultural diversity and supporting small producers whose bottles might otherwise go unnoticed. For many attendees, the event succeeded in turning curiosity into appreciation, underscoring that California’s wine story extends far beyond its most popular grapes. The combination brings out the best of both varietals. Its aroma is of apricots, peaches and fresh baked bread. The medium-bodied palate The rare Bourboulenc from the Rhone Valley performs well in California • 2024 Acquiesce Bourboulenc $37 This is one of the 13 grapes that are permitted for use in Chateauneuf du Pape in the Rhone Valley. Hints of melon, almond, and graphite accent notes of lime zest, peach and tangerine on the nose. It’s medium bodied to full-bodied, somehow broad and crisp at the same time, with a velvety texture and a savory finish. • 2024 Pali Orange Muscat “Enz Vineyard” $35 It may be hard to track this wine down as only 35 cases were made and it is stunning. A charming nose of honeysuckle, gardenia and orange blossoms jumps out of the glass. You anticipate a sweet wine but on the palate, it is bone dry with apple, mango and citrus flavors. It is deeply layered and complex finishing long, savory and satisfying. This is a delicious grape that deserves to be more widely vinified. • 2024 Rideau Roussanne $52 Roussanne is one of the main white grapes from the Southern Rhone region in France and is used to make white Chateauneuf du Pape. This version from the Santa Ynez Valley starts with a powerful bouquet of jasmine, peach and pears, followed by a satiny seamless palate. It finishes with a balanced, uncommonly bright and tangy finish enlivened by a persistent undertone of minerality. Perfect to accompany roast chicken. • 2023 Acorn Gruner Veltliner $32 Hailing from the Allegria Vineyard in the Russian River Valley this is a noble effort to replicate the national grape of Austria here in California. The wine is textural and floral, with orange blossom, lavender, slate and lemon rind. The wine is structured and chalky, with a savory drift through the middle palate, which draws out the fruit and exotic spice through the finish. Great acidity keeps the wine fresh and inviting. Red Wines Grown on limestone soils the Brosseau Grenache shows great character • 2023 Brosseau Grenache $40 Hailing from a limestone vineyard in the remote Chalone appellation in the Gavilan Mountains, the Brosseau Grenache is a stunning example of the varietal. The wine boasts wonderfully pure cherries on the nose plus hints of herbs and dried spices. Medium-bodied it manages to be both firm and silky-textured at the same time, demonstrating great length and adding seductive shadings of anise and cloves on the finish. This lovely wine, reminiscent of a Chateau Rayas Chateauneuf de Pape, is ready to drink now but will last for at least a decade in the cellar. • 2023 St. Amant Alicante Bouschet $26 (Best Value) Alicante Bouschet was once widely planted in California often mixed with Zinfandel in a field blend. This comes from a Lodi vineyard originally planted in 1922. The wine is dark, almost opaque and feels young and lively. It is textbook Alicante This beautiful Alicante Bouschet from Lodi is the best value wine Bouschet with notes of wild berries, herbs and spices, an earthy and rustic touch and oodles of character. This underappreciated grape deserves more exposure and will continue to improve in the cellar for a long time. • 2023 Ottavino St. Laurent Ricci Vineyard $60 This wine epitomizes what the Festival of Undiscovered Grapes is all about. I have not only never tasted the St. Laurent grape, and I have never even heard of it. It originated in Austria and is grown only at the Ricci Vineyard in the Carneros region. It has a heady, sharp, boysenberry aroma and a bright cherry fruit flavor, light and fruity sort of like a beefy Pinot Noir. Delightful! • 2023 JMC Cellars Teraldego $37 Hailing from the Alto Adige region in northern Italy the Teraldego grape offers a bright and punchy profile with wild cherry, tart plum, leather and rose scents. It has a fragrant and delicate personality with a light supple body and a tart clean finish. This foodfriendly wine would be a perfect partner to grilled salmon. • 2023 Madrona Petit Verdot $38 A glass-coating opaque purple color, the wine sports an impressive bouquet of exotic spices, violets and blackberry. This sets the stage for a concentrated, robust, intense, nicely proportioned wine that will benefit from 4-5 years of additional cellaring. It should see its 20th birthday in peak form. • 2023 Cairjn Red Table Wine $80 This Paso Robles wine is styled after the powerful red blends of Priorat Spain. Primarily Carignan with some Mourvedre, Cab and Syrah thrown in for complexity. It leads with a darkfruited bouquet with anise, baking spices and a touch of leather. The palate strikes a midpoint between plush generosity and vibrant energy, culminating in a lively, juicy finish underpinned by gentle yet persistent tannins, savory flavors, smoke and a sturdy core of mineral notes. • 2023 Lyons Mourvedre $68 This relatively new winery from the Santa Ynez Valley specializes in Rhone varietals. The 2023 Mourvedre reveals an abundance of flowers (violets?) overlaid with nuances of dark cherries, wild berries, tobacco, spices and what the French affectionately call “animal” (wet dog). Built around full-bodied bright acids and deep blueberry fruit, it features a supple layered texture with ultra refined tannins. It recalls for me some of my favorite Mourvedres from the Bandol region in France. Delicious now it will easily last for a decade. A Rhone style blend from Paso Robles • 2021 Thacher “Relative Strangers” $65 A red field blend from Paso Robles this reminds me of a Grenache/Syrah/Mouvedre blend. It’s scented of blueberries and cherries, baking spices, earth and leather. The full-bodied palate features restrained, earthy flavors framed by juicy acidity and soft tannins with a spicy finish. Great partner to a slab of ribs fresh off the grill. • 2018 CrossHatch Winery “Shading” $50 The Shading is a blend of 50% Grenache, 25% Syrah, and 25% Mourvedre from the Los Olivos District in Santa Ynez Valley. Inky dark in color, the wine shows dusty earth, cherries and licorice on the nose, while the full-bodied palate is supple with a silky texture from the Grenache and an underpinning of black olives from the Syrah. Showing ample richness and length, it is a fun, ebullient wine.

Her husband, Jerome Herrick, and daughters, Marianne Canori and Meredith Johnson, were at her side. Born on August 25, 1944 at Alta Bates Hospital in Berkeley, she was the daughter of Dr. Thomas Richard Hofmann and Mary Hofmann. She attended Anna Head School in Berkeley and graduated from Berkeley High School in 1962. She attended the University of the Americas in Mexico City and later graduated from San Jose State University, specializing in the education of children with autism spectrum disorder. Susan met her husband, Jerome “Jerry,” at Berkeley High School; however, their love story did not begin until several years after graduation when they reconnected through mutual friends. Sue and Jerry were married on May 12, 1973. They soon moved to Piedmont and welcomed daughters Marianne and Meredith. Susan devoted countless hours volunteering in Piedmont schools den Club and the Hoe and Hope Garden Club, continuing her lifelong commitment to preserving and enhancing the beauty of the city she loved. Susan maintained a vibrant community life and was a member of the Town and Country Club, Claremont Country Club, the East Bay Auxiliary of the de Young Museum, the Hill Branch of UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland, the National Charity League, and The Cancer League. Her most cherished role was that of a devoted mother and adoring “Nana” to her five grandchildren. Her loved ones describe her as elegant and refined, thoughtful, creative, and loving. She was the heart of her family and will be profoundly missed. A private celebration of her life is planned in Hawaii, the birthplace of her mother, Mary, and a place filled with some of her happiest memories. Donations in memory of Susan Herrick may be made to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation at www.piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org. That willingness to dwell in ambiguity is one of its strengths. The production design reinforces the mood. Filmed in Athens and carefully dressed to resemble Tehran, the city feels dense and claustrophobic. Street markets, apartments and intelligence offices are rendered with a tactile realism. Dialogue flows in Hebrew, Farsi and English. The trilingual structure adds authenticity and also suspense. Misunderstandings are not simply plot devices. articles.text: The book traces a two-century history of diversity as both an intellectual and institutional principle, beginning in 1810 with Wilhelm von Humboldt’s University of Berlin, where participation by Jews and Catholics was encouraged. The Diversity Principle follows the spread of the idea from person to person since then. Oppenheimer does not plan to celebrate the publication with time off. “I don’t take vacations,” he said. “I don’t think I would have written the book without the help of these remarkable students.” He has two hopes for the book’s impact. First, he wants to broaden the historical understanding of diversity. “I hope that when people are discussing the value of diversity and someone says, this is just a new psychology idea invented in the 1970s to support affirmative action, that other people in the conversation will say, ‘No, no, you’re wrong about that. It goes all the way back to the 19th century. You haven’t read The Diversity Principle, you have a false premise’.” His second goal is to encourage dialogue across political lines. “I hope that this allows me to talk with diversity opponents as well as diversity proponents, that it allows me to be in conversation with people from across the political spectrum.” In a review for Forbes, Marybeth Gasman wrote, “One of the most striking interventions in the book is historical. From Oppenheimer’s perspective, diversity did not begin as a corrective to discrimination. Director Tran Anh Hung, best known for The Scent of Green Papaya, understands how to film faces. There are no rules here, no cosmic flowcharts. He simply watches recognition happen and trusts we will feel its pull. The camera lingers a beat longer than expected; a glance carries more weight than any special effect could. The dialogue is genuinely funny and feels lived-in. There is a running argument about furniture that should not work but does, and Parker’s script understands that humor gives romance oxygen. Without it, eternal love would suffocate under its own seriousness. Where the film strains is in its final act. Parker is asking what choice means if you have already made it before, whether patterns of love become their own prison. The movie edges toward something genuinely unsettling, then leans into near-future technology and explicit explanations just when it had worked best leaving the metaphysics mysterious. Still, there is something quietly defiant about Eternity’s faith in performance. The film finds surprising emotional force in scenes that are nothing more than two people talking across a table. It works because these actors are allowed to inhabit moments rather than illustrate them. Not everything needs to reinvent cinema. Sometimes it is enough for a film to remember what movies used to do well: let actors act, let dialogue breathe, trust that small human exchanges might matter more than spectacle. In an age when romantic leads are often little more than well-lit props moving through digital set pieces, watching three talented actors simply perform feels quietly radical. Eternity.
